content: The inclusion criteria for the study required women aged 19 to 50 years. Exclusion criteria included currently pregnant women, women with no history of labor, and individuals with incomplete analytic data. The duration of breastfeeding was defined as the total period of breastfeeding in a woman’s life. Participants were categorized into four groups based on breastfeeding duration: ≤5 months, 6–11 months, 12–23 months, or ≥24 months. Fasting glucose levels >100 mg/dL or a prior diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), HDL cholesterol <50 mg/dL in women or medication use, and triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL or medication use were also considered. The study assessed the risk of bias, with unclear risk judgments for confounding, participant selection, exposure classification, deviations from intended exposures, incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), outcome measurement, selective reporting, and other biases. Random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), and selective reporting (reporting bias) were also judged as unclear risks. The Odense Child Cohort (OCC) study included mothers who gave birth between June 2010 and October 2013. Exclusion criteria were twin pregnancies and gestation periods of less than 32 weeks. Breastfeeding data were collected weekly via SMS questionnaires, asking mothers about breastfeeding, formula use, and complementary food introduction. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into five groups: 0–3 months (including non-breastfeeding mothers), 4–6 months, 7–9 months, 10–12 months, and >13 months. Outcomes included hospitalization due to infections, with bias risks assessed similarly to the previous study. The Southern Community Cohort Study (SCCS) focused on racial disparities in cancer incidence and mortality. Participants were recruited from Community Health Centers (CHCs) in southeastern U.S. states and through mailed recruitment. Inclusion criteria included ages 40–79 years, English proficiency, and no cancer treatment (excluding non-melanoma skin cancer) in the past year. Women who had been pregnant were asked about the number of pregnancies, live births, and total breastfeeding months. Primary exposures included parity and total breastfeeding months, categorized as none, 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, and >12 months. Outcomes included obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²), with bias risks assessed as unclear. The Nurses’ Health Study (NHS) and NHS II pooled data from female nurses aged 30–55 years and 25–42 years, respectively. Parous women were enrolled to examine breastfeeding’s effect on ovarian cancer risk. Exclusion criteria included prior cancer diagnosis or death before baseline. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed in six-month increments (0, 1–6, 7–11, 12–17, 18+ months). Bias risks were assessed as unclear. The UK Women’s Cohort Study (UKWCS) analyzed breast cancer risk in relation to lifetime breastfeeding duration. Data were collected in two phases (1995–1998 and 1999–2002), with 61,000 women responding at baseline and 12,453 completing the second phase. Women with cancer at enrollment were excluded. The study identified 1,762 incident breast cancer cases, with a mean recruitment age of 54 years. Bias risks were judged as unclear. The Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey collected data on pregnant women in 33 randomly selected barangays in Metropolitan Cebu, who gave birth between May 1983 and April 1984. Breastfeeding data were collected at birth and every two months until 24 months. Breastfeeding duration was defined as the age when breastfeeding stopped or the last known breastfeeding age if >24 months. Bias risks were assessed as unclear. A retrospective cohort study in Kurdistan, Iran, included postmenopausal women referred for bone mineral density (BMD) measurement via DXA between 2012 and 2015. Exclusion criteria included nulliparity, no breastfeeding, premature ovarian failure, smoking, and various chronic diseases or conditions affecting bone mass. Breastfeeding duration for each child was obtained through detailed questionnaires. Bias risks were judged as unclear. A cross-sectional study in São Paulo, Brazil, evaluated children and adolescents aged 6–14 years in a private school. Mothers completed a structured questionnaire on breastfeeding occurrence and duration, categorized as never breastfed, <3 months, 3–5 months, 6–11 months, and >12 months. Outcomes included obesity in children and adolescents, with bias risks assessed as unclear. The SMILE study, a birth cohort in Adelaide, South Australia, recruited 2,147 mothers and 2,181 children between July 2013 and August 2014. Data collection included questionnaires, 24-hour recalls, food records, and dental examinations. Breastfeeding duration was determined by asking mothers if their child was currently receiving breast milk and, if not, the age at which breastfeeding stopped. Bias risks were judged as unclear. The Philippine Early Childhood Development Project enrolled children aged 0–4 years in disadvantaged municipalities. Follow-ups were conducted annually, with breastfeeding duration evaluated through maternal recall. Children were categorized into five breastfeeding duration groups: 0–5 months, 6–11 months, 12–17 months, 18–23 months, and ≥24 months. Bias risks were assessed as unclear.
